abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Produced water (PW) derived from petroleum and natural gas extraction operations encompasses hazardous BTEX compounds (benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene, and xylenes), thereby posing significant ecological threats when released into marine ecosystems. This investigation explores the bioremediation capabilities of mixed marine algal culture in conjunction with the isolated strain Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 for the degradation of BTEX in seawater environments. Typical BTEX concentrations in produced water range from 1 to 15 mg/L, depending on geological and operational factors, which justifies the selection of 2.5, 5, and 10 mg/L as representative test conditions. Both experimental systems exhibited vigorous growth and substantial removal efficiencies at BTEX concentrations of 2.5, 5, and 10 mg/L. The mixed algal culture accomplished a significant percentage removal of benzene (%ηbenzene) up to 96% for benzene, whereas Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 demonstrated higher percentage o-xylene removal efficiency (%ηo-xylene) of 95%. Significantly, Tetraselmis sp. adapted effectively to the stress induced by BTEX compounds, emerged as the dominant species within the mixed culture, and consistently exhibited removal capabilities across all BTEX constituents. The comparative analysis indicated that while mixed cultures facilitate broad-spectrum degradation, the isolated Tetraselmis sp. strain delivers targeted efficiency, resilience, and scalability conducive to practical applications in the field. These results highlight the promising potential of marine microalgae, especially Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 as sustainable agents for the bioremediation of BTEX compounds. This study enhances the understanding of eco-friendly treatment methodologies for PW, with consequential implications for coastal conservation and the advancement of a circular bioeconomy.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Produced water (PW) is a massive industrial wastewater generated from oil and gas extraction (Rahman et al. 34; Intelligence 18; Alsarayreh et al. 8). This water is naturally present within the oil reservoir and is being generated during the hydrocarbon extraction stage (Lin et al. 27). Reports show that more than 250 million barrels of PW are generated per day from the gas and oil industries. More than 40% of this huge volume is released into the environment, posing a serious environmental danger (Rahman et al. 34; Intelligence 18). There is no constant volume of PW in oil and gas generation, as it depends on the geographic location of the field and the geological formation (Duraisamy et al. 33). BTEX (benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene, and xylenes), heavy metals, total dissolved solids (TDS), chemical additives used in oil production, and polyaromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) are among the harmful organic and inorganic chemicals found in PW beside other pollutants (Duraisamy et al. 33; Jiménez et al. 22; Zhang et al. 44; Igunnu and Chen 17; Wei et al. 40). If these complex contaminants aren't treated, they can impact water bodies, soil, and the air, posing challenges in treating and reusing the enormous volumes of PW water due to their wide spectrum (Fakhru’l-Razi et al. 13; Varjani et al. 39) and soil (Adipah 1).

Discharging treated PW is permitted within specified standard quantities. However, over time, such discharge may potentially lead to chronic toxicity, posing challenges in accurately measuring its impact on the environmental ecosystem (Wei et al. 40; Al-Ghouti et al. 3; Ali et al. 4). As the volumes of PW are anticipated to rise in combination with the expansion of the oil and gas industries, researchers have increasingly focused on the advantages of treating, recycling, and reusing PW. They have underscored the benefits of implementing new and cost-effective treatment technologies (Jiang et al. 20). It became crucial to find an efficient way to re-utilize this water in a feasible way that can help in terms of environment and sustainability.

Various studies have shown that conventional treatment processes consisting of physical, chemical, and biological unit operations could be used for produced water treatment to achieve the possible recycling and reuse (Riley et al. 35; Freedman et al. 14; Kiss et al. 23). The unit operations used in the treatment process consist of primary and secondary treatment steps, including solid settling, oil separation, and emulsion removal using gravity settling and dissolved air floatation (Wei et al. 40; Jiménez et al. 21; Mousa 31). Chemical unit operations such as coagulation and flocculation are used to improve contaminant removal by enhancing solid separation, while the removal of organic matter is accomplished in the biological process. The poor performance of this treatment process does not permit effective recycling or reuse. Other physiochemical treatment technologies such as flash distillation, freeze–thaw evaporation (Ghafoori et al. 15) floatation (Igunnu and Chen 17), density-based separation, adsorption technologies, membrane (Wei et al. 40), chemical precipitation (Fakhru’l-Razi et al. 13), chemical oxidation, and electrochemical methods (Ghafoori et al. 15) were applied for PW treatment. However, due to high energy requirements (e.g. thermal method), a requirement for pre- and post-treatments (e.g. membrane & adsorption), the generation of sludge and its disposal complications (e.g. chemical precipitation, electrochemical systems), and very low efficiency limited the application of these technologies and highlighted the need for other feasible technologies.

Algae technology plays an essential role in the treatment of produced water by removing or utilizing harmful chemicals and pollutants (Camarillo and Stringfellow 12; Sudmalis et al. 37). Although different hazardous components in PW might inhibit microalgae, the rich nutrient content of nitrogen and phosphorus in the form of ammonium and phosphate can promote the algae growth (Hassanien et al. 16). Consequently, employing microalgae in the treatment of PW can positively affect the removal of pollutants such as nutrients, heavy metals, and dissolved and complex organic chemicals, while contributing to CO2 bio-capturing and producing biomass (Alsarayreh et al. 8). Therefore, cultivating microalgae in PW is an environmentally friendly method that has the potential to purify this wastewater for potential recycling and reutilization.

Recent studies have extensively explored the use of algal-based biomass for water treatment. However, despite these efforts, there remains a notable gap in knowledge concerning the cultivation of microalgae in real PW, the treatment of PW with microalgae, and the potential of PW bioremediation with native algae. Moreover, limited information is available regarding the resistance capacity and toxicity of PW to undergo effective degradation. There is limited availability of studies on the use of Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 in BTEX treatment. The potentiality of microalgae in the bioremediation of hydrocarbons, particularly BTEX compounds, has been rigorously examined in different studies. For example, Li and Meng (24) elucidated that the freshwater microalga Chlorella vulgaris can degrade as much as 85% of benzene from a synthetic medium when subjected to mixotrophic conditions. In a parallel investigation, the tolerance and removal efficacy of a Scenedesmus consortium within the context of industrial wastewater. Additionally, Takáčová et al. (38), conducted a thorough examination of the enzymatic pathways implicated in toluene degradation by Pseudokirchneriella subcapitata. While these investigations affirm the foundational concept of phycoremediation for BTEX, it is noteworthy that the majority have been executed in controlled laboratory settings or with freshwater species. There exists a significant deficiency in research regarding the effectiveness of marine microalgae within complex, high-salinity environments, such as produced water (PW). Additionally, fewer studies and less extensive research may be available on the utilizing Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 and mixed algal culture in the degradation of BTEX. This study aims to evaluate and compare the BTEX degradation efficiency of mixed marine algal cultures and the isolated strain Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152, identifying the most resilient and effective candidate for sustainable produced water treatment. Specifically, this study aims to evaluate the capacity of local marine algae and an isolated Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 for treating PW in Qatar, with a particular focus on the removal of BTEX (Benzene, Toluene, Ethylbenzene, and Xylene). In addition, there is a clear gap in understanding the efficiency of indigenous microorganisms in degrading BTEX chemicals, especially concerning hydrocarbon contamination in marine ecosystems. Thus, assessing the potential of this microorganism as a valuable resource for mitigating hydrocarbon pollution is of great importance. Furthermore, this research aims to contribute to the field of environmental bioremediation by presenting a case study that demonstrates the effectiveness of an indigenous microorganism in addressing hydrocarbon contamination on a global scale. Therefore, the study seeks to identify suitable local marine microalgae strain capable of simultaneously capturing CO2, treating PW, producing biomass, and adding value to the ecosystem. Prior investigations have examined BTEX degradation utilizing bacterial consortia and freshwater algae; however, marine microalgae have yet to be thoroughly investigated despite their adaptability to saline conditions. For instance, Chlorella vulgaris and Scenedesmus obliquus have demonstrated moderate BTEX degradation under controlled laboratory settings, although their efficacy diminishes in saline produced water matrices (Ruiz-Marin et al. 36; Ajala and Alexander 2). This research seeks to fill that void by assessing a marine strain, Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152, sourced from the Arabian Gulf, which exhibits superior tolerance and targeted degradation capabilities for o-xylene.

sec.title: Chemicals
sec.p: Benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene, p-xylene, o-xylene, and dichloromethane (each with a purity > 99%) were purchased from Sigma Aldrich and used as received without further modification.

sec.title: Algae cultivation culture
Algae cultivation in BTEX
sec.p: Experiments were conducted to assess specific algal proliferation rates (μ, day⁻1), dry cell biomass (DCW, g/L), and the efficacy of BTEX removal (%ηBTEX). Cultures were cultivated in 500 mL Erlenmeyer flasks that were sealed with Teflon-lined screw caps. Each flask was filled with 300 mL of seawater that had been inoculated with algae and was subjected to continuous illumination via white, fluorescent lamps for a duration of 24 h. Homogeneous mixing was achieved through constant agitation at a rate of 120 rpm utilizing an IKA C-MAG HS7 magnetic stirrer.

BTEX solutions were formulated to replicate typical contamination levels found in produced water, drawing from established literature values. The targeted concentrations included 2.5 mg/L, 5 mg/L, and 10 mg/L of total BTEX, which corresponded to individual compound concentrations of benzene (0.7, 1.4, 2.8 mg/L), toluene (0.6, 1.2, 2.4 mg/L), ethylbenzene (0.4, 0.8, 1.6 mg/L), p-xylene (0.4, 0.8, 1.6 mg/L), and o-xylene (0.4, 0.8, 1.6 mg/L), respectively. Control flasks contained algal cultures in seawater devoid of BTEX addition, maintained under identical experimental conditions.

After the BTEX degradation assays, the leading algal strain was rigorously isolated and purified for advanced analytical methodologies. Colonies showing recognizable morphological features were streaked onto BG11 agar plates to promote the establishment of pure cultures. The isolated strain was stored at 28 °C and then propagated in BG11 medium for acclimatization. Systematic microscopic analyses were conducted utilizing high-resolution instrumentation (Primo Star ZISS AxioCam HRc and Primo Plan ANCHROMAT 100×/1.25 oil) to assess growth and morphological attributes.

The isolation process substantiated the predominance of Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 through microscopic examination and colony purification techniques. Its efficacy was further checked in pure culture experiments conducted under equivalent BTEX conditions for comparative assessment. This strain demonstrated considerable potential for utilization of BTEX bioremediation as well as in diverse wastewater treatment techniques.

sec.title: Genomic DNA extraction and PCR purification of the isolated Tetraselmis_sp. QUCCCM152
sec.p: The genomic DNA extraction of the isolated strain was carried out using the PureLinkTM Plant kit (Sigma, USA) for total DNA purification. Polymerase Chain Reactions (PCR) of the 16SrDNA gene were performed using both EAE3 (5′ TCGACAATCTGGTTGATCCTGCCAG 3′) and N1200R (5′ AACATCTAAGGGCATCACAGAC CTG 3′) primers. The PCR amplification followed the protocol of the GenJet Gel extraction kit (Thermo Scientific, USA). Sequence analysis was conducted using the BLASTn tool, and similarities were identified upon comparison with sequences in the GenBank dataset.

sec.title: BTEX analysis
sec.p: The BTEX compounds were analyzed using Gas chromatography- mass spectroscopy (GC–MS) to quantify and identify each compound by measuring its molecular weight. Extraction of BTEX from the culture medium was carried out using a 1:1 volume ratio of dichloromethane solvent. The mixture was agitated for 20 min at a shaking speed of 180 rpm using a KS 501 orbital shaker and then centrifuged at 7000 rpm for 5 min. The upper layer containing the extracted compounds was transferred to chromatograph vials and stored at 4 °C in a refrigerator for subsequent quantification. To ensure accurate analysis, a solution with high purity was prepared to create a calibration curve. The assessment of BTEX compounds was performed using a Clarus SQ 8S gas chromatograph, which incorporates an Elite column (30 m × 0.25 mm × 1.0 µm), adhering to the analytical guidelines provided in the cited methodology. The analysis was carried out using electron impact ionization mode, and the oven temperature was programmed in the following manner. It commenced with an initial heating phase at 50 °C for 0.5 min, followed by a ramping rate of 15 °C per min until it reached a final temperature of 170 °C, which was maintained for 1.5 min. The maximum temperature was capped at 350 °C, and helium gas was employed as the carrier at a flow rate of 1 mL/min for 0.4 min, subsequently transitioning to 0.7 mL/min for 0.7 min. Subsequently, the BTEX constituents were separated from the algae for precise concentration assessment (Method 30B: Volatile Organic Compounds by Gas Chromatography, Mass Spectrometry (GC, MS) 30).

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analysis was conducted to examine the degradation of various concentrations of BTEX by a mixed algae culture over a specified period. A Two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was employed for this purpose. The normality of the data was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test, while variance homogeneity was examined via the Brown-Forsythe test. Significance of differences was determined using the Holm-Sidak technique, with multiple comparisons conducted at a significance level of p < 0.05. The statistical analysis was carried out using SigmaPlot 14.0 software. All experiments were conducted in triplicate (n = 3). Statistical significance was determined using two-way ANOVA with Holm-Sidak post hoc tests (p < 0.05). Significant differences are indicated in the figures using asterisks or letter groupings.

sec.title: Influence of BTEX concentrations
sec.p:
The experimental procedures were carried out in two successive phases: the preliminary degradation of BTEX utilizing a mixed algal culture, followed by the isolation and independent evaluation of the predominant strain Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 under congruent conditions. GC–MS was used for quantification of BTEX compounds, and different peaks were observed at different retention times to indicate the molecular weights of compounds present such as benzene (78, 2.73 min), toluene (92, 3.81 min), ethylbenzene (106, 4.95 min), and p-xylene and o-xylene (106, 5.07 and 5.35 min, respectively) Fig. 1. BTEX compounds were extracted from the culture supernatant, not from algal biomass, to assess residual concentrations post-degradation.Fig. 1
GC–MS chromatogram for BTEX compounds showing Retention time and relative Abundance

Figure 1 illustrates the GC–MS chromatogram of BTEX compounds extracted from the culture supernatant. The distinct peaks at retention times of 2.73, 3.81, 4.95, 5.07, and 5.35 min correspond to benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene, p-xylene, and o-xylene, respectively. The clear separation of these peaks confirms the presence of BTEX in the untreated samples, establishing a baseline for evaluating subsequent biodegradation performance.

Figure 2a and c illustrates the effect of varying concentrations of BTEX (Benzene, Toluene, Ethylbenzene, and Xylene) on the specific growth rate (μ, day−1) and dry cell weight (DCW, g/L) in a mixed algal culture. Significant differences in μ curves were observed in control and tested samples across varying BTEX concentrations (2.5, 5, and 10 mg/L). The findings reveal that the mixed algal culture experienced a short lag phase before exponential growth between days 2 and 8. This growth trend was consistent in the control sample and those treated with 2.5, 5, and 10 mg/L of BTEX. The initial optical density (OD) values were recorded as 0.33, 0.32, 0.3, and 0.239 a.u, respectively. In addition, measurements of DCW and μ using Eq. (1–2) were conducted to understand the growth patterns. The control sample exhibited the highest DCW value of 0.63 g/L, followed by the 2.5 and 5 mg/L BTEX samples with DCW values of 0.47 and 0.43 g/L, respectively. However, the growth medium that contains 10 mg/L BTEX sample demonstrated a notably lower DCW of 0.30 g/L, indicating inhibited growth. Moreover, Fig. 2c, demonstrates the growth rate and dry cell weight g/L of Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152. The figures reported the initial optical density (OD) were recorded as 0.183, 0.18, 0.17 and 0.168 a.u, for the control and the samples were treated with 2.5, 5 and 10 mg/L of BTEX, respectively. The control sample achieved the highest value of DCW, which was 0.56 g/L, followed by the 2.5, 5 and 10 mg/L BTEX samples, with DCW values of 0.37, 0.34, and 0.27 g/L, respectively. Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 observed a significant increase in growth curves, as shown in Fig. 2c, with no lag phase before the exponential growth started and an increase in the exponential rate 2–10 days period since Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 algae had already adapted to the presence of BTEX compounds since the strain was dominant in the mixed algal culture following treatment. Tetraselmis is a fast-growing microalgae strain known for its ability to survive in various environments (Borowitzka 11). However, the observed differences in μ values provide evidence of mixed algal culture sensitivity to various concentrations of BTEX compounds, illustrating their negative impact on algal growth, as well as the reduction in DCW and μ when the concentration of BTEX in the growth medium exceeds 10 mg/L. The obtained results highlight the fact that elevated concentrations of BTEX, particularly ≥ 10 mg/L, detrimentally affect algae growth, resulting in a significant decrease in both DCW and μ. Consistent pattern, of µ with values of 0.154, 0.138, 0.133, and 0.101 day−1 for the control sample, followed by the samples with 2.5 mg/L, 5 mg/L, and 10 mg/L BTEX, respectively. While the results obtained for the μ values from Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 recorded 0.159, 0.14, 0.124 and 0.114 day−1, respectively. A significant increase in μ values was obtained in the predominant strain Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 demonstrates the positive effect of preliminary cultivation in the culture medium with different BTEX concentrations before treatment to enhance the growth rate and biomass production. A relative increase in the biomass yield was observed in samples 2.5 and 10 mg/L of BTEX. The superior degradation of o-xylene by Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 can be explained by its enzymatic strength in addressing aromatic ring arrangements and its evolutionarily tailored membrane transport processes, which support the incorporation and biotransformation of hydrophobic substances. On the other hand, the heightened benzene removal observed in the mixed algal culture could be ascribed to synergistic interactions among diverse strains, resulting in a wider metabolic versatility and aiding the co-metabolism of simpler BTEX compounds. The enhanced degradation of o-xylene by Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 implies the existence of specialized enzymatic pathways, which may involve monooxygenases or dioxygenases that initiate the cleavage of the aromatic ring, as suggested in studies concerning other hydrocarbon-degrading microalgae (Li and Meng 24; Li et al. 26). It is imperative to stress that the removal efficiencies indicated in this research are associated with the net reduction of BTEX concentrations found in the aqueous phase. Although biological degradation is generally regarded as the predominant metabolic pathways employed by Tetraselmis sp. remain to be established, and the influence of alternative processes, such as the adsorption by algal cells or abiotic volatilization, was not specifically quantified (Takáčová et al. 38; Mazzeo et al. 29). An extensive elucidation of the intracellular degradation pathways represents a critical domain for forthcoming research, potentially employing transcriptomic or metabolomic approaches. It’s important to highlight the clear correlation between the presence of organic molecules and their potential influence on biomass yield and μ, as evidenced in Table 1, resulting in an increased biomass yield and growth rates comparable to those observed in the study. The biomass yield exhibited a considerable increase in the 2.5 and 5 mg/L samples compared to the biomass yield for medium containing 10 mg/L of BTEX. The results of this study indicate that the algae demonstrated the capacity to thrive in seawater containing different concentrations of BTEX, thus showing their resilience to these organic chemicals. Although optical density measurements were graphed over a temporal scale Fig. 2a and c), the growth rate parameters (μ) were derived from the exponential growth phase (days 2–8) and are comprehensively presented in Table 1. The specific growth rate μ, day -1 and biomass yield YDCW yield (g/L). The 28-day endpoint was employed for microscopic examination and strain isolation, coinciding with the stabilization of BTEX degradation trajectories. The study conducted by Ammar et al. (9) observed notable μ of Nannochloropsis Oculata and Isochrysis Galbana strains when cultivated in different percentages of produced water (0%, 10%, 25%, and 50%). The observed values of μ were 0.15, 0.152, 0.179, and 0.123 day−1, respectively. Comparably, it was shown that Isochrysis Galbana exhibited biomass productivity of 0.144, 0.169, 0.158, and 0.132 day−1 when treated to similar concentrations of PW. AlMomani and Örmeci (7) reported μ values of 0.55, 0.31, and 0.68 day−1 for C. vulgaris and N. oleoabundans grown in primary effluent, secondary effluent, and centrate at a temperature of 36 °C. Lutzu and Dunford (28) used various microalgae strains to treat flowback wastewater. It was observed that the strains Amphora coffeaformis, Tetraselmis striata, and Geitlerinema amphibium exhibited lower values of μ compared to the present study, with values of 0.1, 0.08, and 0.1, respectively. The DCW were found to be 0.4 g/L, 0.4 g/L, and 0.6 g/L, respectively. Ammar et al. (9) reported that Nannochloropsis oculata exhibited higher growth and adaptation capabilities compared to Isochrysis galbana when cultivated in different concentrations of PW. Moreover, the biomass of Nannochloropsis oculata was observed to vary at different concentrations of PW. Specifically, the biomass concentration of Nannochloropsis oculata was found to be 1.123, 1.0166, 0.856, and 0.31 g/L for PW concentrations of 0%, 10%, 25%, and 50% respectively. Similarly, it was demonstrated that Isochrysis galbana had biomass productivity of 1.01, 0.899, 0.638, and 0.314 g/L under the same concentrations, respectively. Parsy et al. (32) proposed that Nannochloropsis oculata exhibits robust growth capability in seawater with PW concentrations ranging from 10 to 30% v/v, while the study noted a decrease in the value of μ for Isochrysis galbana when PW concentration exceeded 40% v/v. The maximum growth rates attained were 0.35, 0.27, and 0.16 day−1. Similarly, Nannochloropsis oculata also experienced a decline in growth rate as the PW concentration ≥ 40% v/v, with the maximum growth rates attained being 0.35, 0.27, and 0.16 day−1. Almomani et al. (5) showed that the DCW productivity for three different species Spirulina platensis (SP.PL), Chlorella vulgaris (Ch.v), and mixed microalgae (M.X) cultivated in a municipal wastewater treatment were 0.88, 0.75, and 0.93 g/L, respectively. Japar et al. (19) investigated the impact of acclimation on the growth of four different species of microalgae (Chlorella vulgaris, Chlorella sorokiniana UKM3, Chlamydomonas sp. UKM6, and Scenedesmus sp. UKM9) grown in anaerobic digested palm oil mill effluent (POME) at concentrations ranging from 10 to 30% v/v. The biomass productivity varies across species specifically, Chlorella vulgaris showed a significant rise in biomass yield (Ydcw, g/L) when POME concentration reached 30% v/v. The Ydcw for the four species were follows as Chlorella vulgaris, 1.58 g/L, Chlorella sorokiniana UKM3, 1.87 g/L, Chlamydomonas sp. UKM6 1.68 g/L, and Scenedesmus sp. UKM9 1.46 g/L. (5) showed when Spirulina platensis (SP.PL) and mixed indigenous microalgae (MIMA) were cultivated in wastewater under ambient conditions, the maximum DCW was in the range 0.796 to 0.950 g/L per day. Upon comparing the findings from existing literature with those achieved in the present study, it becomes evident that variations in DCW are influenced by various factors, including algal species, the type of wastewater utilized for cultivation, and the availability of sufficient nutrients in the growth medium. Furthermore, cultivation conditions, such as temperature, pH levels, and continuous stirring to prevent algal settling and sticking, are revealed to exert a significant influence on treatment efficiency and processes. Notably, the results of DCW measurements play a crucial role in determining biomass content and subsequent biomass harvesting for biofuel production.

The present study examined samples for their ability to grow in the presence of different BTEX concentrations added to the culture. However, results indicated a negative correlation between the concentrations of BTEX and the biomass dry weight, resulting in a reduction in biomass as the BTEX concentrations increased. Increasing the concentration of BTEX significantly impacted the final biomass and algae growth rate. Based on the data obtained, Fig. 2b demonstrates a gradual decrease in dry biomass over time for mixed culture samples. However, Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152, as shown in Fig. 2d increases the growth rate and biomass production.

sec.title: Identify the dominant strain adapted after the treatment process
sec.p:
This part of the study examined the effectiveness of a mixed algal culture (consisting of several strains of microorganisms) in treating PW containing varying quantities of BTEX. The goal was to study the interaction of these strains and assess their collective effect on improving the biodegradation of BTEX chemicals. The combined effort of these strains significantly enhanced the breakdown of BTEX, as shown in Fig. 3a and b, offering an understanding of the development of algal cultures in BTEX treatment. The cells appear dispersed in a fluid medium, suggesting active growth or adaptation during the early phase of BTEX treatment. Microscopic assessments were carried out on days 0, 14, and 28 to determine modifications in community composition. Quantitative assessments from numerous fields of view revealed that Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 comprised more than 80% of the total population by day 28, thereby substantiating its prevalence. This designated timepoint was identified because of the stabilization detected in both biomass and BTEX removal trends. In addition to morphological identification, genomic analysis was performed to confirm the identity of the isolated strain, which is done by amplification of the 16S rDNA gene from the isolated strain. A BLASTn analysis conducted on the sequenced polymerase chain reaction (PCR) product revealed a 100% congruence with the GenBank accession number OL764499. Consequently, the isolate was classified as Tetraselmis sp. strain QUCCCM152. After 28 days of treatment, the original mixed algal culture changed, leading to the development of a particular surviving species known as Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 (Fig. 3c). In addition, switching from a mixture of algae cultures to Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 offers a chance to utilize this strong species in upcoming research on PW treatment. Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 became the dominant species after the successful bioremediation process, showing potential for isolating and defining algae for various bioremediation purposes in different wastewater treatments. Hence, Tetraselmis sp. has been considered a microalgae strain that is rapidly growing, and its ability to thrive across extensive salinity ranges has attracted its potential as a promising and sustainable source for biofuel production (Becker 10). Moreover, various Tetraselmis species were reported as promising, sustainable, and eco-friendly approaches in wastewater treatment and heavy metal removal (AlMomani and Örmeci 7). Using a combination of several types of algae in treating wastewater shows potential as an environmentally friendly method that is cost-effective, energy-efficient, and sustainable. The results obtained in this section establish a basis for stimulating further research on the topic.Fig. 3
Micrographs of algal cultures. a, b Mixed microalgal culture observed at different magnifications c The microalga Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 observed at high magnification

sec.title: BTEX degradation by mixed culture algae and Tetraselmis sp QUCCCM152
sec.p:
The results of % removal efficiency (%η) illustrated in Fig. 4 show %ηBenzene, ηToluene, ηEthylbenzene, η-p-xylene, and ηo-xylene by the mixed algal culture sample within a period of 4 days. As shown in the Fig. 4, the mixed culture successfully degraded all BTEX compounds. Also, the concentration of BTEX gradually decreased during the degradation process, demonstrating that although the BTEX mixture influences algae growth, they still possess the ability to degrade contaminants and achieve excellent ηBTEX. According to Fig. 4a, at a BTEX concentration of 2.5 mg/L, Benzene had the most effective removal capability among the BTEX compounds, achieving a notable %ηBenzene of 96%. A descending trend in removal efficiency was observed, with benzene being most effectively degraded (96%), and o-xylene showing the lowest removal rate (65%). Nevertheless, the highest ηBTEX for wastewater with initial BTEX concentrations of 5 and 10 mg/L were slightly decreased as shown in Fig. 4b and c. The %ηbenzene, %ηtoluene, %ηethylbenzene, %η p-xylene, and %ηo-xylene were found to be 88, 87, 80, 65, and 44% for BTEX concentration of 5 mg/L. Lower %ηo-xylene were observed for a concentration of 10 mg/L, being 77, 58, 35, and 39%, respectively. The observed %ηBTEX values are greater than those of Tetraselmis sp QUCCCM152 as compared to mixed algal culture (Fig. 5). There was a decrease %ηBenzene of (~ 59%), %ηToluene of (~ 69%), and %ηEthylbenzene of (~ 72%) for BTEX concentration of 2.5 mg/L as shown in Fig. 5a. Interestingly, the %ηP-xylene of (~ 82%) and %ηO-xylene of (~ 90%) were notable higher than in the case of mixed culture. Although O-xylene is frequently cited as the most resistant compound among BTEX (Lutzu and Dunford 28), the %η O-xylene by Tetraselmis sp QUCCCM152 were found to be higher than mixed algal culture. Furthermore, higher %ηO-xylene of ~ 95% by Tetraselmis sp QUCCCM152 was achieved at a concentration of 10 mg/L (You et al. 43), the highest %ηBTEX achieved using Rhodococcus sp. ZJUT312's was recorded as ηO-xylene followed by ethylbenzene, toluene, benzene, m-xylene, and p-xylene. The results revealed that the degradation rate of o-xylene reached a maximum value of 0.117 mmol L−1 h−1. Wongbunmak et al. (41) showed that the strain M. esteraromaticum SBS1-7 exhibited a comparable degradation capability for o-xylene compared to other isomers of xylene. The results in Fig. 5b and c demonstrate that Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 can reduce BTEX concentration at different concentrations (e.g. 5 and 10 mg/L), achieving %ηbenzene, %ηtoluene, %, %ηp-xylene, and η o-xylene of 63%, 71%, and 82% and 76%, respectively. The variation in the initial algal cell biomass and culture conditions explained the differences observed in the η results obtained in this study and the literature, as suggested (AlMomani and Örmeci 6).Fig. 4
Removal efficiency of BTEX (%ηBTEX) using mixed algal culture a 2.5 mg/L, b 5 mg/L, c 10 mg/LFig. 5
Removal efficiency of BTEX (% ηBTEX) using Tetraselmis sp QUCCCM152 a 2.5 mg/L, b 5 mg/L, c 10 mg/L

Wongbunmak et al. (41) observed that M. esteraromaticum can efficiently break down all components of BTEX, whether present together or separately. The degradation tests were conducted for 5 days to determine the remediation of the BTEX contaminants. Based on the findings, ethylbenzene exhibited a higher %ηethylbenzene during biodegradation when it was part of a BTEX mixture compound. The enhancement of %ηethylbenzene in the presence of additional BTEX compounds suggests a synergistic effect between %ηethylbenzene and other BTEX compounds. This increase in degradation can be attributed to the greater biomass, likely fueled by the availability of preferred growth substrates such as toluene and m-xylene. In this research, Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 was employed to achieve the highest %ηethylbenzene within four days of the degradation process. Up to 82% of %ηethylbenzene was attained with a 5 mg/L concentration of BTEX, compared to %ηethylbenzene of 80% achieved with a mixed culture.

Wongbunmak et al. (42) revealed that Bacillus amyloliquefaciens subsp. Plantarum strain W1 can degrade all six BTEX compounds, whether used individually or in combination. However, the %η m-xylene and %η o-xylene was slightly enhanced when they were present alongside other BTEX compounds, suggesting a possible induction effect induced by these additional components. The complete removal of the BTEX compounds was achieved after a 24-h biodegradation, indicating that Bacillus amyloliquefaciens W1 could degrade all BTEX compounds when provided as the sole substrate. Li et al. (26) conducted a study on the bioremediation of p-xylene using an isolated microalgae Rhodomonas sp. JZB-2 (Cryptophyta), revealing a limited range of species capable of degrading p-xylene. Specifically, Rhodomonas sp. JZB-2 demonstrated the ability of 30 mg/L of %ηp-xylene over 6 days, albeit with a noticeable decrease in growth kinetics. Consequently, they determined that an optimal concentration for biodegradation was 9.682 mg/L of p-xylene. This difference in biodegradation values underscores the efficiency and capability of their algal strains in degrading the BTEX mixture, despite the absence of strains specifically tailored for p-xylene degradation.

Mazzeo et al. (29) observed that Pseudomonas putida could degrade all BTEX compounds in raw wastewater from petroleum refineries. The study revealed that benzene, toluene, and ethylbenzene were completely consumed at low BTEX concentrations, suggesting Pseudomonas putida's effectiveness in reducing various BTEX concentrations. This indicates successful removal of all BTEX compounds by the microorganisms studied from the raw petroleum refinery effluent in the presence of BTEX. Comparing this study to previous research, only the examined mixed algal culture strain showed a %ηbenzene of 96% and a %ηtoluene of 93% at a concentration of 2.5 mg/L of BTEX. In contrast, Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 exhibited a significantly higher %ηp-xylene of 95% when exposed to a concentration of 10 mg/L BTEX.

The findings of this study show that Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 and mixed marine algal culture were shown to have a promising %ηBTEX and the capacity to thrive in BTEX medium. Moreover, the results showed that Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 demonstrated a substantial %ηBTEX of each compound independently. However, mixed cultures are more resilient to potentially harmful components in industrial waste. In addition, there was a significant decrease in the concentration of BTEX compounds in the samples over four days following the use of biodegradation as a remediation technique. Therefore, utilizing a mixed culture strain proves to be effective in remediating BTEX contamination in the PW.

Figures 6a–e and 7a–e depict the decrease in concentrations of BTEX compounds at 2.5, 5, and 10 mg/L, alongside the respective percentage of removal (%η) for each compound by utilizing a mixed algal culture and Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152, respectively. Figure 6a illustrates the %ηbenzene as a function of time at different initial concentrations (2.5, 5, and 10 mg/L). Results revealed that the %ηbenzene values after one day of incubation were 68%, 21%, and 22%, respectively. According to the results, %ηBenzene is influenced by increased BTEX concentration. Significantly, after 4 days, the %ηbenzene values increased to 96%, 87%, and 75% for 2.5, 5, and 10 mg/L, respectively. The outcomes obtained by employing mixed culture exhibited higher %ηbenzene. When comparing the results obtained from Tetraselmis sp QUCCCM152, it was found that the percentages of the outcomes were 32%, 23%, and 14% at concentrations of 2.5, 5, and 10 mg/L, respectively (Fig. 7a).Fig. 6
Removal efficiency of a %ηBenzene, b %ηToluene, c %ηEthylbenzene, d %ηp-Xylene, e %ηO-xylene using mixed algal cultureFig. 7
Removal efficiency of a %ηBenzene, b %η Toluene, c %ηEthylbenzene, d %ηp-Xylene, e %ηO-xylene through Tetraselmis sp QUCCCM152

Figure 6d and e illustrate a decline in the efficacy of mixed algae in degrading o-xylene and p-xylene when 5 and 10 mg/L BTEX were added into the culture. The highest values of %ηO-xylene and %ηP-xylene were 44% and 39%, respectively. Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 removed 95% and 90% of %ηp-xylene and %ηo-xylene at 2.5 and 10 mg/L (Fig. 7d and e), respectively, while a decline was observed at 5 mg/L concentration, reaching 76% and 53%, respectively. Takacova et al. (38) showed that the microalgae Parachlorella kessleri were utilized to bioremediate a BTEX mixture in synthetic petroleum effluent. Over 72 h, significant reductions in BTEX levels were observed. %ηToluene exhibited the highest removal of 63%, while the %ηethylbenzene was 30% after 72 h. Notably, %ηbenzene and %ηxylenes decreased to 64% and 56%, respectively, within 48 h. In contrast to this study, toluene obtained similar results, a %ηToluene of 63% was achieved using Tetraselmis sp QUCCCM152 after 72 h, and %ηToluene of 89% utilizing mixed algal culture.

This finding highlights the efficacy of utilizing a mixed culture strain and Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 for the remediation of BTEX contaminants. The results indicate their potential to remove all BTEX compounds (%ηBTEX) at different concentrations (2.5,5 and 10 mg/L). In addition, a notable and substantial %ηBTEX of BTEX compounds was observed. Furthermore, BTEX concentrations were reduced in the samples from the first to the fourth day during the biodegradation process.

Thus, this finding highlights the efficacy of utilizing a mixed culture strain to remediate BTEX contaminants. However, there is a limited availability of studies on the use of Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 in BTEX treatment. Additionally, fewer studies and less extensive research may be available on utilizing Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 and mixed culture are used in the degradation of BTEX. As a result, Tetraselmis sp QUCCCM152 demonstrates enhanced growth in a BTEX medium and biomass production. According to the study, using a mixed culture strain can improve the removal efficacy (%η) of BTEX compounds, making it a viable method for remediating organic pollutants.

While this investigation elucidates the substantial efficacy of a combination of mixed marine algae and Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 in the degradation of BTEX compounds under meticulously controlled laboratory conditions, the transition to real-world produced water (PW) treatment systems poses numerous challenges. Our experimental framework was established within batch cultures utilizing synthetic BTEX amalgams in seawater, which do not adequately reflect the intricate nature of actual PW, inclusive of variable salinity, pH levels, and the occurrence of inhibitory co-contaminants such as heavy metals and polyaromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) (Jiménez et al. 22; Al-Ghouti et al. 3; Ali et al. 4). The application of this methodology to pilot-scale systems, including open ponds or photobioreactors, necessitates optimization concerning light penetration, gas exchange, and the harvesting of biomass, while concurrently ensuring the resilience of the introduced strains against the indigenous microbial community (Alsarayreh et al. 8; Camarillo and Stringfellow 12; Sudmalis et al. 37). Tackling these scale-up impediments in future research employing continuous-flow systems and authentic PW is imperative for substantiating the commercial feasibility of this promising bioremediation strategy.

In summary, while the mixed algal culture demonstrated broader degradation capacity, Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 exhibited targeted efficiency and resilience, particularly under o-xylene stress. These findings support its potential as a robust candidate for scalable BTEX bioremediation in marine PW environments.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This study demonstrates the potential of marine microalgae for BTEX bioremediation in produced water. The mixed algal culture achieved up to 96% benzene removal, while the isolated strain Tetraselmis sp. QUCCCM152 showed 95% o-xylene removal and maintained consistent degradation across all BTEX components. Growth rate analysis revealed that Tetraselmis sp. adapted well to BTEX stress, with a maximum specific growth rate of 0.159 day⁻1 and biomass yield of 0.451 g/L in control conditions. These findings highlight the strain’s resilience and suitability for scalable, eco-friendly treatment of hydrocarbon-contaminated wastewater.
